feed.title: BIP54: On fixing time-warp and the (unsoundness) of the forward block idea

entry.title: BIP54: On fixing time-warp and the (unsoundness) of the forward block idea
entry.summary:
The proposal known as "forward blocks" suggests the introduction of a parallel blockchain, termed the "forward chain," to serve as a novel transaction ordering mechanism. In this construction, blocks on the forward chain are periodically anchored into the main compatibility chain once a designated depth is reached, ensuring that any reorganization of the forward chain would necessitate a corresponding reorganization of the compatibility chain. Once transactions in the forward chain achieve sufficient confirmations, they are added to a shared transaction queue accessible by both chains. To prevent the forward chain from surpassing the processing capabilities of legacy compatibility chain nodes, congestion in the transaction queue triggers a slowdown in block production on the compatibility chain, prompting a subsequent reduction in mining difficulty and allowing it to catch up. This synchronization process leverages the existing MTP (Median Time Past) mechanism to act as a scalability constraint.
Despite its innovative approach, the forward block idea raises significant cryptoeconomic concerns, particularly regarding the necessity to process transactions twice—once on the forward chain and again on the compatibility chain—unless users pay transaction fees twice for the same transaction. The foundational intuition behind the proposal relies on leveraging the time-warp bug's adjustment malleability to increase block throughput during periods of congestion. However, with BIP54 introducing stricter timestamp rules, this malleability becomes more constrained but not entirely eliminated. Post-BIP54, miners retain a window of 7,200 seconds within which block timestamps can be manipulated, translating to a modest potential increase in block capacity and rate by approximately 0.60 percent. Such changes, while still feasible, would undermine the efficiency gains anticipated by the original forward block proposal due to these increased constraints.
A key assumption made by the proposal is that transactions included in forward blocks could adhere to newer consensus rules, maintaining their visibility to older nodes while limiting their ability to validate these transactions meaningfully. If this assumption holds, transaction data from the forward chain could theoretically be compressed into zero-knowledge proofs, which are then committed to the compatibility chain, trading off data size for computational complexity and shifting the bottleneck from time to storage or bandwidth. Nevertheless, even with such optimizations, non-upgraded nodes would face increased bandwidth and disk space requirements, potentially threatening network decentralization. The scale of capacity increase suggested by the proposal, such as producing one compatibility block every 167 milliseconds, is unrealistic given practical limitations like network latency and the risk of adversarially slow validation.
Security implications further complicate the forward chain model. The design envisions increasing block rewards on the forward chain at the expense of those on the compatibility chain, yet the finality and security of the forward chain remain dependent on the compatibility chain. This leads to inefficiencies where two sets of validators must duplicate processing efforts for the same transactions, while fee rewards are not proportionally increased unless users pay double fees. The loosely coupled nature of state synchronization means that validators, whether upgraded or not, bear higher validation costs, as they must handle the state generation on the forward chain and then synchronize it on the compatibility chain, both for the same reward. This creates an environment where capacity growth comes at the expense of significantly heightened validation costs per transaction, raising the risk of denial-of-service attacks since there is no guarantee that increased capacity will be matched by proportional fee revenues to compensate validators for their additional work.
Given these trade-offs, it is proposed to include a footnote in the BIP54 document elucidating why the forward block idea does not present a sufficiently secure or practical solution for the Bitcoin network. It is considered reasonable to reduce the surface area of time-warp vulnerabilities in light of these findings, and a mitigation strategy should accompany this recommendation. While the forward block concept remains scientifically intriguing, especially for its exploration of theoretical consensus mechanisms, its practical shortcomings outweigh its potential benefits under current network conditions. For reference, further technical details and discussions on this topic can be found in the relevant paper at [https://lists.linuxfoundation.org/pipermail/bitcoin-dev/2019-July/017054.html](https://lists.linuxfoundation.org/pipermail/bitcoin-dev/2019-July/017054.html).
